Let me search for more information about the latest satellites to provide a comprehensive comparison. I'll look for information about Starlink satellites and other modern satellite systems.

Based on my search, I can now provide you with a detailed comparison between the first satellite and the latest satellite technology.

## First Satellite: Sputnik 1 (1957)

**Sputnik 1**, launched by the Soviet Union on **October 4, 1957**, was humanity's first artificial satellite. It was remarkably simple by today's standards:

| Feature | Specification |
|---------|---------------|
| **Size** | 58 cm (23 inches) in diameter |
| **Weight** | 83-84 kg |
| **Shape** | Metal sphere with four external antennas |
| **Orbit** | Low Earth orbit (230-940 km altitude) |
| **Orbital period** | ~96 minutes |
| **Payload** | Thermometer, radio transmitter, batteries, fan |
| **Mission duration** | 3 weeks (batteries died), remained in orbit until January 1958 |
| **Purpose** | Primarily political/technological demonstration |

Sputnik 1 essentially just emitted radio pulses that allowed tracking—its scientific capabilities were minimal.

---

## Latest Satellites: Modern Systems (2020s)

Today's satellites represent an enormous technological leap. Here are several categories of "latest" satellites:

### 1. **Starlink Satellites (SpaceX)**
- **Weight**: ~260-295 kg each
- **Size**: Compact flat-panel design (~3m x 1.5m when deployed)
- **Function**: Global broadband internet constellation
- **Quantity**: **Over 5,000+ satellites** in orbit (as of 2024)
- **Capabilities**: High-speed data transmission, inter-satellite laser links, autonomous collision avoidance

### 2. **Hubble Space Telescope (for comparison, still operational)**
- **Weight**: 11,110 kg
- **Size**: 13.2m long, 4.2m diameter
- **Function**: Deep-space astronomical observation
- **Capabilities**: Captures images of galaxies billions of light-years away

### 3. **International Space Station (largest artificial satellite)**
- **Weight**: ~440,000 kg
- **Size**: 109m x 73m
- **Function**: Permanent human habitation, scientific research
- **Continuously occupied since 2000**

### 4. **Modern Communications Satellites (e.g., Viasat-3)**
- **Weight**: Up to ~6,000-7,000 kg
- **Orbit**: Geostationary (35,786 km altitude)
- **Capabilities**: Terabit-level data throughput, global internet coverage

---

## Key Comparisons

| Aspect | Sputnik 1 (1957) | Modern Satellites (2020s) |
|--------|-----------------|---------------------------|
| **Weight** | 83 kg | 260 kg (Starlink) to 440,000 kg (ISS) |
| **Size** | Beach ball-sized | Car-sized to football-field-sized |
| **Power** | Batteries (3 weeks) | Solar panels (15+ years) |
| **Function** | Radio beeper | Internet, TV, GPS, weather, science, military |
| **Data capacity** | None (just pulses) | Terabits per second |
| **Lifespan** | 3 weeks operational | 5-15+ years |
| **Cost to build** | Minimal | Millions to billions of dollars |
| **Constellation size** | 1 satellite | Thousands working together |
| **Autonomy** | None | AI-powered operations |
| **Manufacturing** | Hand-crafted | Mass-produced (Starlink: ~120/month) |

---

## The Paradox: Satellites Are Also Getting Smaller

Interestingly, while some satellites have grown massive, the "latest" trend also includes **CubeSats** and **nanosatellites**:
- **Size**: 10 cm cubes (1U CubeSat)
- **Weight**: ~1-4 kg
- **Cost**: Tens of thousands of dollars (vs. Sputnik's enormous Soviet budget)
- **Capabilities**: Often exceed Sputnik's—cameras, radios, scientific instruments

A modern smartphone has more computing power than all of Sputnik's systems combined, and a basic CubeSat can outperform the first satellite in almost every metric at a fraction of the cost.

---

## Summary

The evolution from Sputnik 1 to today's satellites spans roughly **67 years** and represents perhaps the most dramatic technological transformation in any field:
- **5,000× heavier** (ISS vs. Sputnik)
- **Infinite data capacity** comparison (none vs. global internet)
- **From single purpose to multi-function** swarms
- **From weeks to decades** of operational life
- **From national prestige project to commercial commodity**

Yet the fundamental principle remains the same: both use orbital mechanics and radio communication—Sputnik simply proved it was possible.

---

Sources:
1. https://astrobiology.nz/sputnik-1-and-the-space-age/
2. https://darwincav.com/sputnik-1-the-first-artificial-satellite/
3. https://www.spacecapital.com/blogs/satellites-past-present-future
4. https://www.remotesatellite.com/the-exciting-shift-in-satellite-technology/
